claim: Viruses have evolved diverse mechanisms to antagonize host immunity such as direct inhibition and relocalization of cellular APOBEC3B (A3B) by the ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) of Epstein-Barr virus.
source: Viruses have evolved diverse mechanisms to antagonize host immunity such as direct inhibition and relocalization of cellular APOBEC3B (A3B) by the ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) of Epstein-Barr virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is part of the manuscript's introduction of established findings.

claim: Human gamma-herpesvirus RNRs engage A3B via largely distinct surfaces.
source: First, we find that human gamma-herpesvirus RNRs engage A3B via largely distinct surfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation and microscopy experiments shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: RNR-mediated enzymatic inhibition and relocalization of A3B depend upon binding to different regions of the catalytic domain.
source: Second, we show that RNR-mediated enzymatic inhibition and relocalization of A3B depend upon binding to different regions of the catalytic domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deaminase activity assays and microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The capability of viral RNRs to antagonize A3B is conserved among gamma-herpesviruses that infect humans and Old World monkeys that encode this enzyme but absent in homologous viruses that infect New World monkeys that naturally lack the A3B gene.
source: Third, we show that the capability of viral RNRs to antagonize A3B is conserved among gamma-herpesviruses that infect humans and Old World monkeys that encode this enzyme but absent in homologous viruses that infect New World monkeys that naturally lack the A3B gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation, microscopy, and deaminase activity assays shown in Figures 6-8.

claim: The ancestral primate A3B protein is active and similarly engaged by the RNRs from viruses that infect humans and Old World monkeys but not by the RNRs from viruses that infect New World monkeys.
source: Finally, we reconstruct the ancestral primate A3B protein and demonstrate that it is active and similarly engaged by the RNRs from viruses that infect humans and Old World monkeys but not by the RNRs from viruses that infect New World monkeys.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation, microscopy, and deaminase activity assays with reconstructed ancestral A3B shown in Figure 8.

claim: The birth of A3B at a critical branchpoint in primate evolution may have been a driving force in selecting for an ancestral gamma-herpesvirus with an expanded RNR functionality through counteraction of this antiviral enzyme.
source: These results combine to indicate that the birth of A3B at a critical branchpoint in primate evolution may have been a driving force in selecting for an ancestral gamma-herpesvirus with an expanded RNR functionality through counteraction of this antiviral enzyme.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and evolutionary analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A3 genes are unique to placental mammals.
source: A3 genes are unique to placental mammals and the evolutionary history of the A3 locus is marked by frequent expansions and contractions resulting from independent events of gene duplication, loss, and fusion (Münk et al., 2012; LaRue et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2020; Conticello, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The evolutionary history of the A3 locus is marked by frequent expansions and contractions resulting from independent events of gene duplication, loss, and fusion.
source: A3 genes are unique to placental mammals and the evolutionary history of the A3 locus is marked by frequent expansions and contractions resulting from independent events of gene duplication, loss, and fusion (Münk et al., 2012; LaRue et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2020; Conticello, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the primate lineage leading to humans the A3 locus evolved from an ancestral 3 deaminase domain cluster to the present-day 11 domain (7 gene) cluster.
source: For instance, in the primate lineage leading to humans the A3 locus evolved from an ancestral 3 deaminase domain cluster to the present-day 11 domain (7 gene) cluster.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about primate A3 evolution.

claim: A3B may be the youngest A3 family member in primates.
source: Interestingly, phylogenetic and comparative genomics studies indicate that A3B may be the youngest A3 family member in primates (LaRue et al., 2008; Uriu et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A3B was likely generated by the duplication of ancestral deaminase domains in the common ancestor of Catarrhini primates (i.e., hominoids and Old World monkeys) and is consequently absent in Platyrrhini primates (i.e., New World monkeys).
source: Specifically, A3B was likely generated by the duplication of ancestral deaminase domains in the common ancestor of Catarrhini primates (i.e., hominoids and Old World monkeys) and is consequently absent in Platyrrhini primates (i.e., New World monkeys) (depicted in Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: EBV BORF2 and KSHV ORF61 share only ~42% primary amino acid identity.
source: Although sharing only ~42% primary amino acid identity, the predicted model of KSHV ORF61 overlays well with the cryo-EM structure of EBV BORF2 with root mean square deviation of 1.26 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of protein sequences.

claim: The predicted model of KSHV ORF61 overlays well with the cryo-EM structure of EBV BORF2 with root mean square deviation of 1.26 Å.
source: Although sharing only ~42% primary amino acid identity, the predicted model of KSHV ORF61 overlays well with the cryo-EM structure of EBV BORF2 with root mean square deviation of 1.26 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational structural modeling data.

claim: EBV BORF2 and the predicted structure of KSHV ORF61 share a similar sized SHI region, which is lacking in nonviral class Ia RNRs such as those from Escherichia coli and humans.
source: Interestingly, in addition to similar HLS regions, EBV BORF2 and the predicted structure of KSHV ORF61 share a similar sized SHI region (depicted in red in Figure 1C), which is lacking in nonviral class Ia RNRs such as those from Escherichia coli and humans (Shaban et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 1C and cited prior work.

claim: Replacing L7 of A3Bctd or A3A with L7 of A3Gctd completely abolishes interaction with EBV BORF2.
source: As expected from our prior studies, replacing L7 of A3Bctd or A3A with L7 of A3Gctd completely abolishes interaction with EBV BORF2 (Figure 2B, left panel, lanes 1–4)
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Replacing L7 of A3Gctd with L7 of A3A/Bctd endows binding to EBV BORF2.
source: and, reciprocally, replacing L7 of A3Gctd with L7 of A3A/Bctd endows binding (Figure 2B, left panel, lanes 5–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Replacing L7 of A3Bctd or A3A with L7 of A3Gctd does not affect binding by KSHV ORF61.
source: However, we were surprised to find that replacing L7 of A3Bctd or A3A with L7 of A3Gctd does not affect binding by KSHV ORF61 (Figure 2B, right panel, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Replacing L7 of A3Gctd with L7 of A3A/Bctd does not enable pull-down by KSHV ORF61.
source: Accordingly, replacing L7 of A3Gctd with L7 of A3A/Bctd does not enable pull-down by KSHV ORF61 (Figure 2B, right panel, lanes 5–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Replacing L3 of A3Bctd or A3A with L3 of A3Gctd nearly abolishes the interaction with KSHV ORF61.
source: For EBV BORF2, similar pull-down levels are observed for wild-type (WT) versus L3-swapped A3s (Figure 3B, left panel, lanes 1–4), whereas replacing L3 of A3Bctd or A3A with L3 of A3Gctd nearly abolishes the interaction with KSHV ORF61 (Figure 3B, right panel, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Replacing L3 of A3Gctd with L3 of A3A/Bctd is sufficient to promote modest immunoprecipitation with KSHV ORF61.
source: Additionally, replacing L3 of A3Gctd with L3 of A3A/Bctd is sufficient to promote modest immunoprecipitation with KSHV ORF61 (Figure 3B, right panel, lanes 5–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The L3 region is critical for KSHV ORF61 binding and likely to have little or no role in binding to EBV BORF2.
source: These results indicate that the L3 region is critical for KSHV ORF61 binding and likely to have little or no role in binding to EBV BORF2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Replacing L1 of A3A with L1 of A3Bctd leads to a marked increase in EBV BORF2 co-IP.
source: First, we confirmed our recent report by showing that replacing L1 of A3A with L1 of A3Bctd leads to a marked increase in EBV BORF2 co-IP (Figure 4A, left panel, lanes 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Replacing L1 of A3Bctd with L1 of A3A dramatically diminishes the interaction with EBV BORF2.
source: Reciprocally, replacing L1 of A3Bctd with L1 of A3A—but not with L1 of A3Gctd—dramatically diminishes the interaction with EBV BORF2 (Figure 4A, left panel, lanes 4–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: KSHV ORF61 does not appear to bind more strongly to A3Bctd compared to A3A.
source: In contrast, KSHV ORF61 does not appear to bind more strongly to A3Bctd compared to A3A (Figure 4A, right panel, compare lanes 1 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: L1 swaps between A3Bctd and A3A have no effect on KSHV ORF61 co-IPs.
source: Moreover, L1 swaps between A3Bctd and A3A have no effect on KSHV ORF61 co-IPs (Figure 4A, right panel, lanes 1, 2, 4, and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EBV BORF2 strongly inhibits A3B deaminase activity in cell lysates.
source: As expected, EBV BORF2 strongly inhibits A3B deaminase activity in cell lysates as indicated by minimal product accumulation (Figure 5A, left panel, compare lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: KSHV ORF61 inhibits A3B-catalyzed deamination when compared to a no-RNR control, albeit to a considerably lesser extent compared to EBV BORF2.
source: KSHV ORF61 also inhibits A3B-catalyzed deamination when compared to a no-RNR control, albeit to a considerably lesser extent compared to EBV BORF2 (Figure 5A, left panel, compare lanes 1 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neither EBV BORF2 nor KSHV ORF61 substantially inhibits the deaminase activity of A3A.
source: Surprisingly, neither EBV BORF2 nor KSHV ORF61 substantially inhibits the deaminase activity of A3A (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutating EBV BORF2 Y481 to an alanine or a proline effectively prevents inhibition of A3B-catalyzed deamination.
source: Mutating EBV BORF2 Y481 to an alanine or a proline effectively prevents inhibition of A3B-catalyzed deamination, likely by weakening the interaction with the L1 region (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When L1 of A3B is replaced with L1 of A3A, EBV BORF2 completely loses its capacity to inhibit ssDNA deamination.
source: In contrast, when L1 of A3B is replaced with L1 of A3A, EBV BORF2 completely loses its capacity to inhibit ssDNA deamination (Figure 5D, left, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The EBV BORF2 interaction with A3B L1 is a requirement for inhibiting deamination.
source: Nevertheless, these results combine to indicate that the EBV BORF2 interaction with A3B L1 is a requirement for inhibiting deamination and also help explain why A3A activity is not inhibited similarly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only the RNRs from viruses that infect A3B-encoding primates (humans and rhesus macaques) pull-down human A3Bctd and A3A.
source: In support of our hypothesis, only the RNRs from viruses that infect A3B-encoding primates (humans and rhesus macaques) pull-down human A3Bctd and A3A (Figure 6C, lanes 1–4, left and right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The RNRs from viruses that infect primates without A3B (marmosets and squirrel monkeys) are unable to pull down either A3Bctd or A3A.
source: In contrast, the RNRs from viruses that infect primates without A3B (marmosets and squirrel monkeys) are unable to pull down either enzyme (Figure 6C, lanes 5–6, left and right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only the RNRs from viruses that infect A3B-encoding primates are able to relocalize human A3B and A3A from the nucleus to the cytoplasmic compartment.
source: In agreement with our co-IP results, only the RNRs from viruses that infect A3B-encoding primates are able to relocalize human A3B and A3A from the nucleus to the cytoplasmic compartment.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: EBV BORF2 potently inhibits A3B deaminase activity.
source: Consistent with our previous results, EBV BORF2 potently inhibits A3B (Figure 6E, top panel, lane 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The RNR of rhesus macaque Lymphocryptovirus McHV-4 shows similarly strong inhibition of A3B as EBV BORF2.
source: A similarly strong inhibition is seen with the RNR of rhesus macaque Lymphocryptovirus McHV-4 (Figure 6E, top panel, lane 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The RNRs from marmoset Lymphocryptovirus CalHV-3 and squirrel monkey Rhadinovirus SaHV-2 are both defective in inhibiting A3B activity.
source: Most importantly, the RNRs from marmoset Lymphocryptovirus CalHV-3 and squirrel monkey Rhadinovirus SaHV-2 are both defective in inhibiting A3B activity (Figure 6E, top panel, lanes 4 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: None of the six different viral RNRs inhibits the activity of human A3A.
source: Additionally, none of the six different viral RNRs inhibits the activity of human A3A (Figure 6E, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: All four RNRs from viruses that infect Catarrhini primates bind to the A3A enzymes of their respective host species.
source: In line with our results above with human A3Bctd and A3A (Figure 6), all four RNRs from viruses that infect Catarrhini primates bind to the A3A enzymes of their respective host species (Figure 7A, lanes 1, 2, 4, and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The RNRs from viruses infecting New World monkeys are unable to bind to their hosts' A3As.
source: In contrast, the RNRs from viruses infecting New World monkeys are unable to bind to their hosts' A3As (Figure 7A, lanes 3 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The RNRs from CalHV-3 and SaHV-2 do not alter the localization of marmoset and squirrel monkey A3A, respectively.
source: In contrast, the RNRs from CalHV-3 and SaHV-2 do not alter the localization of marmoset and squirrel monkey A3A, respectively (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The chimeric CalHV-3 RNR construct with the HLS region from EBV BORF2 is unable to bind marmoset A3A.
source: Interestingly, although the chimeric CalHV-3 RNR construct is still unable to bind marmoset A3A (Figure 7D, lane 2), this protein is now able to efficiently bind to both human A3Bctd and A3A (Figure 7D, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The chimeric CalHV-3 RNR construct with the HLS region from EBV BORF2 is able to efficiently bind to both human A3Bctd and A3A.
source: Interestingly, although the chimeric CalHV-3 RNR construct is still unable to bind marmoset A3A (Figure 7D, lane 2), this protein is now able to efficiently bind to both human A3Bctd and A3A (Figure 7D, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The HLS region of EBV BORF2 is sufficient to endow a normally non-binding Lymphocryptovirus RNR with a capacity to engage both human A3Bctd and A3A.
source: These results indicate that the HLS region of EBV BORF2 is sufficient to endow a normally non-binding Lymphocryptovirus RNR with a capacity to engage both human A3Bctd and A3A, likely by enabling a direct physical interaction with the identical loop 7 region of these enzymes (L7 region alignment in Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Only the RNRs from gamma-herpesviruses that infect primates with A3B are capable of binding to human A3Bctd.
source: In agreement with results above, only the RNRs from gamma-herpesviruses that infect primates with A3B are capable of binding to human A3Bctd (Figure 8B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Nearly all RNRs from viruses that infect primates with A3B are able to bind the ancestral A3B protein.
source: Similarly, nearly all RNRs from viruses that infect primates with A3B are able to bind the ancestral protein and, importantly, all viruses that infect primates which naturally lack the A3B gene are unable to bind the ancestral enzyme (Figure 8B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All viruses that infect primates which naturally lack the A3B gene are unable to bind the ancestral A3B enzyme.
source: Similarly, nearly all RNRs from viruses that infect primates with A3B are able to bind the ancestral protein and, importantly, all viruses that infect primates which naturally lack the A3B gene are unable to bind the ancestral enzyme (Figure 8B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All RNRs derived from viruses that infect hosts that encode A3B show some capacity to inhibit the ssDNA deamination activity of human A3B.
source: Using a panel of 11 primate gamma-herpesvirus RNRs, we show that, in addition to binding and relocalization, all RNRs derived from viruses that infect hosts that encode A3B show some capacity to inhibit the ssDNA deamination activity of human A3B, but none of these viral proteins could inhibit the deaminase activity of human A3A (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: None of the viral RNRs from viruses that infect hosts that encode A3B could inhibit the deaminase activity of human A3A.
source: Using a panel of 11 primate gamma-herpesvirus RNRs, we show that, in addition to binding and relocalization, all RNRs derived from viruses that infect hosts that encode A3B show some capacity to inhibit the ssDNA deamination activity of human A3B, but none of these viral proteins could inhibit the deaminase activity of human A3A (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The RNR from ColHV-1 shows no ability to bind, relocalize, or inhibit present-day human or ancestral A3B.
source: Interestingly, despite its similarity to KSHV ORF61, the RNR from ColHV-1—a novel KSHV-related virus identified in African Colobinae monkeys (Dhingra et al., 2019)—differs from the RNRs of all other viruses that infect Catarrhini primates tested here in that it shows no ability to bind, relocalize, or inhibit present-day human or ancestral A3B (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, and Figure 8D)
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation, microscopy, and deaminase activity assay data shown in Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, and Figure 8D.

claim: African Colobinae monkeys appear to have lost the A3B gene following the Colobinae subfamily split into the African and Asian tribes 10–14 million years ago.
source: This apparent incongruity may be explained by the fact that African Colobinae monkeys appear to have lost the A3B gene following the Colobinae subfamily split into the African and Asian tribes 10–14 million years ago (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: Evidence for diversifying selection was detected at multiple sites in primate A3B, including clusters of positively selected residues in loops 1 and 3.
source: We detected evidence for diversifying selection at multiple sites, including clusters of positively selected residues in loops 1 and 3 (Figure 8F, top; Figure 8—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 4A–B.

claim: The amino acid composition of loops 1 and 3 in A3B may have been influenced by recurrent diversifying selection, possibly as a mean to escape binding by gamma-herpesvirus RNRs.
source: This suggests that the amino acid composition of these regions may have been influenced by recurrent diversifying selection, possibly as a mean to escape binding by gamma-herpesvirus RNRs, which in turn would select for virus adaptation to restore binding (depicted in Figure 8F, bottom).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: BORF2-null EBV exhibits lower infectivity and an accumulation of A3B signature C/G-to-T/A mutations.
source: The importance of this A3B counteraction mechanism is evidenced by BORF2-null EBV exhibiting lower infectivity and an accumulation of A3B signature C/G-to-T/A mutations (Cheng et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Direct contacts between EBV BORF2 and the L7 region of A3Bctd are essential for this host-pathogen interaction.
source: Recent biochemical and structural studies demonstrated that direct contacts between EBV BORF2 and the L7 region of A3Bctd are essential for this host-pathogen interaction (Cheng et al., 2019b; Shaban et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A3Bctd is closely related to A3A with >90% amino acid identity including identical L7 regions.
source: A3Bctd is closely related to A3A (>90% amino acid identity including identical L7 regions; Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: KSHV ORF61 is capable of binding and relocalizing A3B and A3A, but not other A3 enzymes.
source: Recent work also revealed that KSHV ORF61 is similarly capable of binding and relocalizing A3B and A3A, but not other A3 enzymes (Cheng et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A3B L7 is a critical determinant of EBV BORF2 binding.
source: In agreement with our recent cryo-EM studies (Shaban et al., 2022), we show that A3B L7 is a critical determinant of EBV BORF2 binding, whereas A3B L1 serves to help strengthen this interaction and confer selective binding over A3A (Figure 2 and Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4 and cited prior work.

claim: A3B L1 serves to help strengthen the interaction with EBV BORF2 and confer selective binding over A3A.
source: In agreement with our recent cryo-EM studies (Shaban et al., 2022), we show that A3B L7 is a critical determinant of EBV BORF2 binding, whereas A3B L1 serves to help strengthen this interaction and confer selective binding over A3A (Figure 2 and Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4 and cited prior work.

claim: KSHV ORF61 mainly relies on L3 to bind and relocalize cellular A3B/A.
source: Surprisingly, these same rules do not apply to KSHV ORF61, which appears to mainly rely on L3 to bind and relocalize cellular A3B/A (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The EBV BORF2-A3Bctd interaction has a biolayer interferometry dissociation constant of ~1 nM.
source: The A3B-selective nature of this host-pathogen interaction is orthogonally supported by previous binding studies showing that the EBV BORF2-A3Bctd interaction has a biolayer interferometry dissociation constant of ~1 nM, whereas the interaction with the >90% identical A3A enzyme is over 10-fold weaker (Shaban et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The interaction of EBV BORF2 with the >90% identical A3A enzyme is over 10-fold weaker than with A3Bctd.
source: The A3B-selective nature of this host-pathogen interaction is orthogonally supported by previous binding studies showing that the EBV BORF2-A3Bctd interaction has a biolayer interferometry dissociation constant of ~1 nM, whereas the interaction with the >90% identical A3A enzyme is over 10-fold weaker (Shaban et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The direct binding of EBV BORF2 to two loop regions near the A3B catalytic site—L1 and L7—helps stabilize the BORF2-A3B complex, resulting in a high affinity interaction.
source: It is thus possible that the direct binding of EBV BORF2 to two loop regions near the A3B catalytic site—L1 and L7—helps stabilize the BORF2-A3B complex, resulting in a high affinity interaction and consequently blocking the A3B active site from accessing ssDNA substrates and catalyzing deamination.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Grafting the HLS region from EBV BORF2 into the RNR from marmoset CalHV-3 enables binding to human A3B.
source: Importantly, the potential adaptability of this A3B counteraction mechanism in Lymphocryptoviruses is highlighted by results showing that grafting the HLS region from EBV BORF2—which contains residues that directly contact A3B L1 and L7—into the RNR from marmoset CalHV-3 enables binding to human A3B (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: KSHV ORF61 binding to A3B largely through L3 may result in a lower affinity interaction that more weakly inhibits ssDNA deamination.
source: In comparison, KSHV ORF61 binding to A3B largely through L3 may result in a lower affinity interaction that more weakly inhibits ssDNA deamination.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Binding to the A3 active site by viral RNRs is responsible for both protein relocalization and enzymatic inhibition.
source: These inferences support a model in which binding to the A3 active site by viral RNRs is responsible for both protein relocalization and enzymatic inhibition, yet substantial deaminase activity inhibition is only observed above a certain affinity threshold.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: EBV latency is limited to B lymphocytes.
source: For instance, EBV latency is limited to B lymphocytes (Young and Rickinson, 2004), which can express high levels of endogenous A3B (Koning et al., 2009; Refsland et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: B lymphocytes can express high levels of endogenous A3B.
source: For instance, EBV latency is limited to B lymphocytes (Young and Rickinson, 2004), which can express high levels of endogenous A3B (Koning et al., 2009; Refsland et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The neutralization of A3B is required to preserve EBV viral genome integrity upon lytic reactivation.
source: which can express high levels of endogenous A3B (Koning et al., 2009; Refsland et al., 2010), strongly implying that the neutralization of this enzyme is required to preserve viral genome integrity upon lytic reactivation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited prior work.

claim: The non-catalytic Z2 domain of A3B accounts for this enzyme's distinct nuclear localization.
source: Notably, the non-catalytic Z2 domain of A3B has been shown to account for this enzyme's distinct nuclear localization (Salamango et al., 2018) and association with multiple RNA binding proteins, in addition to allosterically regulating the catalytic activity of the Z1 domain (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The non-catalytic Z2 domain of A3B is associated with multiple RNA binding proteins.
source: Notably, the non-catalytic Z2 domain of A3B has been shown to account for this enzyme's distinct nuclear localization (Salamango et al., 2018) and association with multiple RNA binding proteins, in addition to allosterically regulating the catalytic activity of the Z1 domain (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The non-catalytic Z2 domain of A3B allosterically regulates the catalytic activity of the Z1 domain.
source: Notably, the non-catalytic Z2 domain of A3B has been shown to account for this enzyme's distinct nuclear localization (Salamango et al., 2018) and association with multiple RNA binding proteins, in addition to allosterically regulating the catalytic activity of the Z1 domain (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cooperation between Z2 and Z1 domains accounts for A3B antiviral function.
source: It is therefore plausible that cooperation between Z2 and Z1 domains accounts for A3B antiviral function, possibly by facilitating access to herpesvirus transcription complexes inside the nucleus (e.g., ssDNA exposed in viral R-loop structures; McCann et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from cited prior work.

claim: Bat species encode the largest known A3 repertoire in mammals.
